 Toyota and Lexus Recall More Cars to Replace Takata Airbags
 It’s the latest in a series of recalls of these dangerous airbags, which first started in 2014
 By 
 Keith Barry 
 Senior Autos Reporter 
 November 19, 2026 
 A 2016 Toyota 4Runner SUV
 Photo: Toyota
 Toyota is recalling over 314,000 cars, trucks, and SUVs to replace dangerous passenger-side airbags that could spray metal shards throughout the passenger cabin. These vehicles include:
 • 2002-2010 Lexus SC430 convertibles
 • 2011 Lexus IS250 sedans and convertibles
 • 2017 Lexus GX460 SUVs
 • 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla sedans
 • 2005-2006 Toyota Tundra trucks
 • 2005-2007 Toyota Sequoia SUVs
 • 2016-2017 Toyota 4Runner SUVs
 MORE ON RECALLS 
 Takata Airbag Recall: Everything You Need to Know 
 What a Car Recall Notice Means and What to Do 
 Make Sure the Used Car You Want Doesn't Have an Open Recall 
 We Answer Your Car Recall Questions 
 The faulty airbags, made by the now-defunct Takata Corporation , have been associated with 28 deaths and more than 400 injuries in the U.S. Since 2014, over 67 million faulty Takata airbags have already been replaced in vehicles made by 34 brands, an effort that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has called “the largest and most complex safety recall in U.S. history.” If you own one of these vehicles and it has already had its airbag replaced, you may need another repair.
 High humidity, high temperatures, and time can increase the risk of rupture. Toyota told NHTSA that it is not aware of any injuries related to the airbags in these specific vehicles, but that they have reached the end of their safe service lives and must be replaced.
 To fix the problem, Toyota and Lexus dealerships will replace these dangerous airbags free of charge.
 How to contact the manufacturer: Owners may contact Toyota at 800-331-4331.
 NHTSA campaign number: 26V748. Toyota’s own numbers for this recall are 26TB25, 26TA25, 26LB11, and 26LA11.

 Keith Barry
 Keith Barry has been an auto reporter at Consumer Reports since 2018. He focuses on safety, technology, and the environmental impact of cars. Previously, he led home and appliance coverage at Reviewed; reported on cars for USA Today, Wired, and Car & Driver; and wrote for other publications as well. Keith earned a master’s degree in public health from Tufts University. Follow him on BlueSky @itskeithbarry.bsky.social .
